prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins, from the PROTAC concept to the cereblon mechanism of molecular glues.

statement.case_for: My opening first choice was base editing (B060), and I still regard it as scientifically excellent, but reading the full set of ballots I now think targeted protein degradation (B037) is the stronger prize case. It was ranked by all eight members and placed in the top three by six, which is far broader than any other shortlisted entry. It is a genuine chemical invention: heterobifunctional molecules and glue degraders that hijack an E3 ligase to remove a protein catalytically, which redefines how a small molecule can act. The cereblon discovery also supplies a mechanism for thalidomide, a long-standing chemical and pharmacological puzzle. Independent reproduction is wide, and from my own field I note that regulated protein turnover, including degradation of RNR subunits, is central to dNTP pool control and genome stability, so I can judge the biology of ubiquitin-dependent degradation with some confidence. The PROTAC and glue strands share one idea, induced proximity to the ubiquitin system, which makes a single prize part coherent.
statement.case_against: The attribution is difficult. Eight names are credited and any trio leaves out major contributors: Sakamoto as co-inventor of the first PROTAC, Ciulli for VHL ligands and ternary-complex mechanism, Gray, and Ito and Kim on the cereblon side. The PROTAC and molecular-glue strands arose from different groups and different logic, so a trio that joins them risks looking assembled to fit the three-name limit. Clinical validation is also incomplete, since to my knowledge no PROTAC has been approved, and the committee should not mistake a large pipeline for settled benefit. Base editing (B060), my opening first choice, has cleaner single-laureate attribution in Liu, but it has the smaller opening following (four members) and sits uneasily next to the 2020 CRISPR prize.

responses.point: Crews and Deshaies conceived and first demonstrated heterobifunctional degraders, Handa identified cereblon, and the glue and PROTAC strands may deserve different weight, so the three-person split is a judgement call.
responses.response: I agree with the structure and share the worry about weighting. I think the case holds together because both strands exploit the same principle, recruitment of an E3 ligase to a protein that the drug does not inhibit, and the cereblon finding is what showed that an old drug already acted this way. I would resist treating Ciulli and Sakamoto as footnotes: if the committee cannot defend omitting Sakamoto from a PROTAC citation, a two-part prize (concept plus mechanism) is the honest fallback. Within the three-name limit, I still find Crews, Deshaies and Handa the most defensible trio, because their contributions are earliest and most conceptually decisive.

responses.point: Induced degradation is a robust concept, but with few approved drugs recognition could be premature relative to its full impact; he ranked it eighth and put Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling first.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously, but I do not think approval of a drug is the right test for a chemistry prize. The first PROTAC dates to 2001, the cereblon mechanism to 2010, and many independent groups have reproduced the mechanism and have degraders in late-stage trials. The scientific claim, that proximity to an E3 ligase can drive catalytic removal of a target, is already settled. I would rank B005 as a fully mature and clean two-person case, and it is my second alternative, but it extends a modality honoured in 2010 rather than opening a new one, and that difference is why I place B037 ahead of it.

responses.point: Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (B016) is a clean two-author 1985 invention with four decades of impact and is overdue, while degraders may be a few years early.
responses.response: The attribution for B016 is the cleanest on the list and I do not dispute its originality or durability. My reservation is only that I am less able to judge its scientific standing than colleagues in computational and physical chemistry, and I would defer to you and Professor Linke on its relative rank. I do not accept that being overdue outweighs breadth of support: only four members ranked B016 at all, whereas B037 appeared on all eight ballots. If the committee settles on a two-part prize, I would be open to pairing a clean computational method with a smaller second part, but not at the cost of splitting a three-name limit unnaturally.

responses.point: B037 is a plausible three-person configuration with independent validation and late-stage trials, but one branch would be left out, and B060 base editing with Liu alone is defensible with Nishida and Kondo as a credit question.
responses.response: I agree on both counts. On base editing, I raised the Nishida and Kondo priority question in my own opening ballot and have not resolved it, and the 2020 CRISPR prize makes the chemistry-versus-biology boundary a real question rather than a technicality. That is part of why I have moved B060 to an alternative. I would still defend it if the committee prefers a single-laureate prize with unambiguous leadership.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can justify a three-name trio from eight credited names, in particular leaving out Sakamoto, Ciulli, Gray, Ito and Kim.
Whether PROTACs and molecular glues should be one prize part or two, and how to weigh them if split.
Whether the absence of an approved PROTAC drug is a real maturity problem or only a clinical lag.
Whether base editing (B060) is better treated as chemistry given the 2020 CRISPR prize, and how to handle Nishida and Kondo priority.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work on nucleotide metabolism and genome stability overlaps in topic with base editing (B060) and DNA-repair condensates (B024), but I have no recorded personal, collaborative or institutional tie to any credited person on the shortlist.
